subject: Geography
description: Monsoon mechanism, climatic regions, western disturbance, El Niño / La Niña impacts

questions.stem: India's climate is best described under the Köppen classification as predominantly:

options.option_text: Tropical and subtropical with strong monsoonal rainfall
Temperate maritime, like that of western European coast
Cold polar, comparable to Siberia and northern Canada
Hot arid desert, like that of the central Sahara region

questions.explanation: India's climate — TROPICAL MONSOON (most of the country) + sub-tropical highland in the Himalayas + arid in the Thar + small temperate zones in the high Deccan. Köppen subtypes for India: Aw (tropical savanna — most of India); Am (tropical monsoon — Western Ghats, NE); As (tropical with dry summer — small parts); Cwa (humid subtropical with dry winter — northern plains); BSh (semi-arid — Rajasthan/Saurashtra); BWh (arid — Thar). Pure temperate, polar, or pure desert are NOT dominant.
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: The SOUTHWEST monsoon brings most of India's annual rainfall and arrives because of:

options.option_text: Reversal of pressure as the landmass heats up faster than ocean
A continuous westerly flow from the Atlantic Ocean year-round
The retreat of polar high pressure southward in summer
Diurnal heating of small Himalayan valleys causing local winds

questions.explanation: SW Monsoon mechanism — in summer, the Indian subcontinent heats faster than the surrounding Indian Ocean → low pressure forms over land (Thar / NW India is the focal heat-low). Air over the comparatively cooler Indian Ocean (high pressure) flows toward this low. Coriolis force deflects the southerly flow into a southwesterly. The winds pick up moisture as they cross the warm Arabian Sea + Bay of Bengal → torrential rainfall when they hit the Western Ghats and the Himalayas. Onset around Kerala (1 June nominal). The 'monsoon trough' migrates north as summer progresses. Distractor 2 — Atlantic doesn't drive Indian monsoon. Distractor 3 — polar fronts are too far away. Distractor 4 — local winds, not the monsoon.
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: WESTERN DISTURBANCES are extra-tropical storms originating over which region, that bring winter rain to NW India?

options.option_text: The Mediterranean Sea region around southern Europe
The Indian Ocean equatorial belt south of Sri Lanka
The Arctic region near the Northern Pole ice cap
The Bay of Bengal, off the eastern coast of India

questions.explanation: Western disturbances — extra-tropical low-pressure systems originating in the Mediterranean / Caspian Sea region, riding eastward on the subtropical jet stream. Bring December-March rainfall + snow to Punjab, Haryana, J&K, HP, Uttarakhand. Critical for the rabi (winter) crop — wheat, mustard, gram. About 4-6 western disturbances per winter, with year-to-year variation. Climate change is altering their frequency + intensity. Distractor 2 — Indian ocean storms are different (cyclones). Distractor 3 — Arctic systems too far north. Distractor 4 — Bay of Bengal cyclones move WESTWARD, into east coast.
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: EL NIÑO is associated in India with which typical monsoon outcome?

options.option_text: Strongly above-average rainfall and timely seasonal onset
Below-normal rainfall and frequent drought conditions
Strong cyclonic activity in the Bay of Bengal alone
Earlier onset of southwest monsoon over Kerala state

questions.explanation: EL NIÑO — periodic warming of the eastern equatorial Pacific (off Peru/Ecuador). Disrupts the normal Walker Circulation, weakens trade winds, and tends to suppress Indian monsoon → drought in India. Major Indian drought years coincided with strong El Niño: 1965, 1972, 1987, 2002, 2009, 2015. LA NIÑA — opposite: cooler eastern Pacific → typically better Indian monsoon. INDIAN OCEAN DIPOLE (IOD) — independent factor; positive IOD favours Indian monsoon (warm western IO, cool eastern), can offset El Niño effect (e.g., 2019 saw +ve IOD compensating for moderate El Niño). MJO (Madden-Julian Oscillation) — intra-seasonal driver.
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: Which Indian region receives the LARGEST share of its annual rainfall from the NORTH-EAST (RETREATING) monsoon, between October and December?

options.option_text: Punjab and Haryana plains in the northwest
Tamil Nadu and southern Andhra coast
Kerala and Karnataka along the western coast
Assam and other NE Indian hill states

questions.explanation: TAMIL NADU and adjoining Pondicherry / coastal AP receive ~50% of their annual rain from the NE monsoon (October-December) — the 'retreating monsoon'. Mechanism — by October, the SW monsoon retreats; high pressure builds over land; cool dry winds blow from NE; pick up moisture over the warm Bay of Bengal; deposit rain on the WINDWARD east coast (TN). Coromandel coast = Coro-mandel = TN + adjacent. Distractor 1 — Punjab/Haryana get most rain from SW monsoon. Distractor 3 — Kerala/Karnataka are heavily dependent on SW monsoon. Distractor 4 — Assam/NE: SW monsoon dominates. Cyclones often develop in the Bay of Bengal during NE monsoon period.
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: MAWSYNRAM in Meghalaya holds the record for one of the highest average annual rainfalls in the world. The reason is mainly:

options.option_text: Tropical convection only, with no orographic effect at all
Moisture-laden winds forced upward by the Khasi Hills (orographic)
A persistent low-pressure cell that lingers over the area year-round
Glacial meltwater rising as humid air to feed daily rainfall there

questions.explanation: Mawsynram — Meghalaya, ~11,872 mm annual average (often the world's wettest, occasionally edged out by Cherrapunji nearby). Reason: SW monsoon winds carry moisture from the Bay of Bengal, funnel into the narrow trough between the Garo and Khasi hills, are forced upward (orographic lift), cool, condense, rain. Cherrapunji (Sohra) and Mawsynram are the two long-standing record holders. Most rain falls during SW monsoon (June-September). Distractor 1 — orographic IS the dominant effect. Distractor 3 — persistent low isn't the mechanism. Distractor 4 — no glaciers there.

options.option_text: Holiday period when Indian schools shut for monsoon rest
A short interruption in the rainfall during the SW monsoon season
Final retreat of southwest monsoon in late September
A complete failure of the entire monsoon over India

questions.explanation: MONSOON BREAK — relatively dry spell of several days (sometimes 2-3 weeks) during the active SW monsoon period when rainfall stalls over the Indian heartland but moves either north (towards the Himalayan foothills) or south (towards the equatorial Indian Ocean). Caused by the monsoon trough shifting its position. Long monsoon breaks during sowing season can damage kharif crops; if late, they can be welcome for harvest. Active vs break phases of the monsoon are the subject of intensive forecasting. Distractor 1 = vacation, not climate. Distractor 3 = monsoon retreat (different phenomenon). Distractor 4 = monsoon failure (full-season deficit, more serious).
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: The hot, dry, dust-laden winds blowing from the west and north-west during May–June across the Indo-Gangetic Plain are locally known as?

options.option_text: Kalbaisakhi — fierce pre-monsoon thunder squalls of Bengal
Loo — scorching dry summer winds of the north Indian plains
Andhis — convective dust storms common over the Rajasthan plains
Blossom showers — pre-monsoon rains aiding coffee plant blooms

questions.explanation: Loo is the correct term for hot, dry westerly winds that blow across the Indo-Gangetic Plain in May–June, often causing heat-stroke conditions. Kalbaisakhi refers to violent nor'wester thunderstorms of West Bengal — quite the opposite of dry winds. Andhis are dust storms of Rajasthan and are convective in origin, not sustained westerly winds like the Loo.

questions.stem: Which pre-monsoon local phenomenon, characterised by violent nor'wester thunderstorms with gusty winds and sudden heavy rain, provides welcome relief to West Bengal and Assam in April–May?

options.option_text: Loo — hot and dry westerly wind blowing over the north Indian plains
Kalbaisakhi — nor'wester storm bringing sudden cooling and heavy rain
Andhis — evening dust storms arising over the arid Thar desert belt
Mango showers — light pre-monsoon rains that aid mango fruit ripening

questions.explanation: Kalbaisakhi (meaning 'calamity of the month of Baisakh') are violent nor'wester thunderstorms that strike West Bengal, Assam and Bangladesh in April–May, bringing sudden cooling. They are caused by the meeting of dry northwest air with moist Bay of Bengal air. Andhis are dust storms of Rajasthan, not eastern India, and Loo is a dry wind — neither brings rain.

questions.stem: A 'positive Indian Ocean Dipole' (positive IOD) event typically produces which effect on India's southwest monsoon rainfall?

options.option_text: Below-normal monsoon rainfall due to cooler western Indian Ocean surface
Above-normal monsoon rainfall due to warmer western Indian Ocean surface
Delayed monsoon onset over Kerala followed by an unusually rapid advance
No significant effect since the Pacific ENSO signal fully dominates monsoon

questions.explanation: In a positive IOD, sea-surface temperatures in the western Indian Ocean (Arabian Sea side) are warmer than normal while the eastern IO is cooler. This enhances moisture and convection over India, favouring above-normal monsoon rainfall. Option A reverses the IOD–monsoon relationship. The IOD is an independent driver and can even partially offset an El Niño-induced deficit, so Option D is wrong.

questions.stem: Pre-monsoon showers arriving in Kerala and Karnataka in March–April that are specifically critical for triggering the flowering of coffee and pepper plantations are called?

options.option_text: Mango showers — pre-monsoon rains that assist mango ripening in summer
Blossom showers — pre-monsoon rains that induce coffee-plant flowering
Kalbaisakhi — violent pre-monsoon thunderstorms typical of eastern India
October heat — oppressive humid spells along the coast after monsoon exit

questions.explanation: Blossom showers (March–April) are distinct from mango showers (April–May): blossom showers trigger flowering in coffee and pepper plantations of Kerala and Karnataka, making them agriculturally critical for plantation crops. Mango showers occur slightly later and are associated with mango ripening, not coffee. This distinction is a classic exam trap, often tested in IBPS and SSC papers.

questions.stem: The India Meteorological Department (IMD) designates which calendar date as the 'normal' onset date of the southwest monsoon over Kerala, used as the official benchmark for monsoon tracking each year?

options.option_text: 25th May — early pre-monsoon showers marking the start of transition
1st June — the IMD-established standard normal onset date over Kerala
10th June — when the monsoon trough typically covers all peninsular India
15th June — the traditional date the monsoon crosses the Konkan coast

questions.explanation: IMD recognises 1 June as the normal onset date of the southwest monsoon over Kerala, based on long-period climatological averages. An onset before this date is 'early', after it is 'delayed'. 25 May is pre-monsoon thunderstorm activity, not the official monsoon onset. 10 June is closer to when the monsoon advances to cover most of the peninsula, not the Kerala onset benchmark.

questions.stem: The Mascarene High, a semi-permanent subtropical anticyclone in the southern Indian Ocean, primarily contributes to the Indian southwest monsoon mechanism by?

options.option_text: Generating western disturbances delivering winter rain to northwest India
Driving the cross-equatorial Somali Jet that channels moisture toward India
Pushing the ITCZ northward past the Himalayas to trigger monsoon breaks
Strengthening El Niño via warm-water pool buildup in the south Indian Ocean

questions.explanation: The Mascarene High (centred near 30°S) acts as the pressure engine that drives air northward across the equator. This cross-equatorial flow is deflected eastward by the Coriolis force to form the low-level Somali Jet (Findlater Jet), the primary moisture conveyor belt of the southwest monsoon. Western disturbances originate from Mediterranean troughs, not this anticyclone. El Niño arises from equatorial Pacific dynamics, unrelated to the Mascarene High.

questions.stem: The northward retreat of which upper-atmospheric jet stream from over the Indian subcontinent to north of the Himalayas in late May–early June is considered the decisive trigger for the onset burst of the southwest monsoon over Kerala?

options.option_text: Tropical Easterly Jet — upper-level eastward current at 150 hPa over India
Somali Jet — intense low-level cross-equatorial flow feeding the Arabian Sea
Subtropical Westerly Jet — upper westerly that retreats poleward in early June
Polar Front Jet — mid-latitude westerly stream linking western Europe to Asia

questions.explanation: The Subtropical Westerly Jet (STJ) lies over northern India (~25°N at 200 hPa) in winter, suppressing convection and keeping conditions dry and stable. Intense heating of the Tibetan Plateau in late May drives the STJ northward beyond the Himalayas (~40°N), removing the atmospheric cap and triggering explosive monsoon convection — the 'burst' of the monsoon. The Tropical Easterly Jet develops after monsoon onset (not before), making Option A a classic trap. The Somali Jet is a low-level moisture feeder, not the upper-level stability switch.
